# Combinations of Transformations

## Combinations of Transformations

> **Spec point** — `1.4`

## Combinations of transformations

### What are combinations of graph transformations?

- When you alter a function in certain ways, the effects on the graph of the function can be described by geometrical transformations
- In additional to single transformations, you need to be able to interpret the effects of multiple transformations applied to the same function

![Combinations What Is, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/94466d35822a-2-10-combinations-what-is.png)

### How do I combine two or more graph transformations?

- Make sure you understand the effects of individual **translations**, **stretches**, and **reflections** on the graph of a function (see the previous pages)
- When applying **combinations** of these transformations, apply them to the graph **one at a time** according to the following guidelines:

  - First apply any **horizontal** transformations **inside** the brackets (if you have more than one transformation inside the brackets, **translations** must be applied **before** **stretches and reflections**)
  
    - *y *= *k*f(***a****x ***+ *****b***)+ *c*
    - For your exam you will only be given **at most one inside** the bracket
  - Then apply any **vertical** transformations **outside** the brackets (if you have more than one transformation outside the brackets, **stretches and reflections** must be applied **before translations**)
  
    - *y *= ***k***f(*ax *+ *b*)**+ *****c***** **
- If the transformation involves a modulus

  - First apply any transformations **inside the modulus sign**
  - Then apply the **effects of the modulus**
  - Then apply any transformations **outside the modulus sign**

![Comb Xforms Modulus Illustration](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/fb02a0f450bc-2-10-comb-xforms-modulus-illustration.png)

- Any ***asymptotes*** of the function are also affected by the combined transformation (perform the transformations one at a time in the same order as above)

> **Exam Hint**
> - Be sure to apply transformations in the correct order – applying them in the wrong order can produce an incorrect transformation.
> - When you sketch a transformed graph, indicate the new coordinates of any points that are marked on the original graph.
> - Try to indicate the coordinates of points where the transformed graph intersects the coordinate axes (although if you don't have the equation of the original function this may not be possible).
> - If the graph has asymptotes, don't forget to sketch the asymptotes of the transformed graph as well.

> **Worked Example**
> ![Comb Xforms Example, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/9fff9d0e7267-2-10-comb-xforms-example.png)

title: Composite Functions
bodyMd:
# Composite Functions

## Composite Functions

> **Spec point** — `1.2`

## Composite functions

### What is a composite function?

- A **composite function **is where one function is applied after another function

![Language of Functions Notes Diagram 8, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/3dd120f9b69f-2-8-1-language-of-functions-notes-diagram-8.png)

- The ‘**output’** of one function will be the ‘**input’** of the next one
- Sometimes called **function-of-a-function**
- A composite function can be denoted

  - $fg(x)$
  - $f(g(x))$
  - $f \left[g \left(x\right)\right]$
  - $(f\circg)(x)$
  - All of these mean “$f$ of $g(x)$”

![Composite Functions Notes Diagram 1, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/4da8ed2c98f3-2-8-2-composite-functions-notes-diagram-1.png)

### How do I use composite functions?

![Composite Functions Notes Diagram 2, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/6871fdd6407a-2-8-2-composite-functions-notes-diagram-2.png)

- **Recognise** the notation The order matters

  - **fg(x)** means **“f **of** g **of** x”**

  - First apply *g *to *x *to get $g(x)$
  - Then apply *f* to the previous output to get $f(g(x))$
  - Always start with the function **closest to the variable**
  - $fg(x)$ is not usually equal to $gf(x)$

### What are special cases of composite functions?

![Composite Functions Notes Diagram 3, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/4ee894a88c77-2-8-2-composite-functions-notes-diagram-3.png)

- **fg(x)** and **gf(x)** are generally different but can sometimes be the same
- **ff(x)** is written as **f**<sup>**2**</sup>**(x)**
- Inverse functions **ff**<sup>**-1**</sup>**(x) = f**<sup>**-1**</sup>**f(x) = x**

> **Exam Hint**
> - **Domain** and **range** are important.In **fg(x)**, the ‘output’ (range) of **g** **must** be in the domain of **f(x), s**o **fg(x)** could exist, but **gf(x)** may not (or not for some values of x).

> **Worked Example**
> ![Composite Functions Example Diagram, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/b7f5c63cdff0-2-8-2-composite-functions-example-diagram.png)

title: Inverse Functions
bodyMd:
# Inverse Functions

## Inverse Functions

> **Spec point** — `1.2`

## Inverse functions

### What is an inverse function?

- An **inverse** **function** is the **opposite** to the original function
- An inverse function is denoted by $f^{-1}(x)$
- The **inverse** of a function only exists if the function is **one**-to-**one**
- Inverse functions are used to solve equations

  - The solution of $f(x)=5$ is $x=f^{-1}(5)$

** **

![Inverse Functions Notes Diagram 1, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/b0d17fe99370-2-8-3-inverse-functions-notes-diagram-1.png)

### How do I sketch the graph of an inverse function?

![Inverse Functions Notes Diagram 2, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/0e4cf13db29a-2-8-3-inverse-functions-notes-diagram-2.png)

- The graphs of a function and its inverse are reflections in the line** y = x**

### What is the domain and range of an inverse function?

![Inverse Functions Notes Diagram 3, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/fa2296ccd75d-2-8-3-inverse-functions-notes-diagram-3.png)

- The range of a function will be the domain of its inverse function
- The domain of a function will be the range of its inverse function

### How do I find an inverse function using algebra?

- Set **y = f(x)** and make **x** the subject
- Then rewrite in function notation
- Domain is needed to fully define a function
- The range of **f** is the domain of **f**<sup>**-1**</sup> (and vice versa)

![Inverse Functions Notes Diagram 4, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/5677c0309536-2-8-3-inverse-functions-notes-diagram-4.png)

### How are inverse functions related to composite functions?

- A function (**f**) followed by its inverse (**f**<sup>**-1**</sup>) will return the input (**x**)
- **ff**<sup>**-1**</sup>**(x) = f**<sup>**-1**</sup>**f(x) = x **(for all values of x)

** **

![Inverse Functions Notes Diagram 5, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/5de03798c57b-2-8-3-inverse-functions-notes-diagram-5.png)

bodyMd:
# Language of Functions

## Language of Functions

> **Spec point** — `1.2`

## Language of functions

### What language is used with functions?

- The language of functions has many keywords associated with it that need to be understood

![Language of Functions Notes Diagram 1, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/37d441053a3d-2-8-1-language-of-functions-notes-diagram-1.png)

### What are mappings?

- A **mapping** takes an ‘**input’** from one **set** of values to an ‘**output’** in another

![Language of Functions Notes Diagram 2, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/9aae11cc3a56-2-8-1-language-of-functions-notes-diagram-2.png)

- Mappings can be

  - ‘**many**-to-**one’** (**many** ‘input’ values go to **one** ‘output’ value)
  - ‘**one**-to-**many’**
  - ‘**many**-to-**many’**
  - ‘**one**-to-**one’**

![Language of Functions Notes Diagram 3, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/894cc04e6163-2-8-1-language-of-functions-notes-diagram-3.png)

### What is the difference between a mapping and a function?

- A **function** is a mapping where every ‘input’ value maps to a **single** ‘output’
- **Many**-to-**one** and **one**-to-**one** mappings are functions
- **Mappings **which have** many possible outputs **are** not functions**

![Language of Functions Notes Diagram 4, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/26ef82e1a3f2-2-8-1-language-of-functions-notes-diagram-4.png)

### What is function notation?

- Functions are denoted by the notation** f(x)**, **g(x)**, etc

  - eg. f(x) = x<sup>2</sup> - 3x + 2
- Or the alternative notation

  - eg. f : x ↦ x<sup>2</sup> – 3x + 2

### What sets of numbers do I need to know?

- Functions often involve domains and ranges for specific sets of numbers
- All numbers can be organised into different sets ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, ℝ

![Language of Functions Notes Diagram 5, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/0ed91f399495-2-8-1-language-of-functions-notes-diagram-5.png)

- So ℕ is a **subset** of ℤ etc
- ℤ<sup>-</sup> would be the set of negative integers only

### What is the domain of a function?

- The **domain** of a function is the set of values that are allowed to be the ‘input’

![Language of Functions Notes Diagram 6, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/b32b439c21f8-2-8-1-language-of-functions-notes-diagram-6.png)

- A function is only fully defined once its domain has been stated
- **Restrictions** on a domain can turn **many**-to-**one** functions into **one**-to-**one** functions

![EXTRA No1, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/c7f1c39b93cd-2-8-1-extra-no1.png)

### What is the range of a function?

- The **range** of a function is the set of values of all possible ‘outputs’ ![Language of Functions Notes Diagram 7, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/e3dd6226f7b5-2-8-1-language-of-functions-notes-diagram-7.png)
- The type of values in the range depend on the domain

![Ui7OQwtV_2-8-1-extra-no2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/6a53d51520bb-ui7oqwtv-2-8-1-extra-no2.png)

# Sketching Graphs of Modulus Functions

## Modulus Functions - Sketching Graphs

> **Spec point** — `1.3`

## Sketching graphs of modulus functions

### What is the modulus function?

- The **modulus** function makes **any** ‘input’ **positive**
- **|x| = x   if x ≥ 0   |f(x)| = f(x)   if f(x) ≥ 0**
- **|x| = -x if x < 0   |f(x)| = -f(x)   if f(x) < 0**

  - **For example: **|5| = 5 and |-5| = 5
- Sometimes called **absolute value**

### How do I sketch the straight line modulus graph y = a|­x+p|+q?

- The graph will look like a “ꓦ” if *a *> 0 or a “ꓥ” if *a *< 0
- There will be a vertex at the point (-*p*, *q*)
- There could be 0, 1 or 2 roots

  - This depends on the location of the vertex and the orientation of the graph (ꓦ or ꓥ)
- Compare this to the **completed square form** of a **quadratic** *a*(x* *+ *p*)² + *q*

![1-2-4-modulus-functions--sketching-graphs-notes-diagram-0](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/9cad09be74cb-1-2-4-modulus-functions-sketching-graphs-notes-d.png)

### How do I sketch the modulus of a function y = |f(x)|?

STEP 1        Pencil in the graph of **y = f(x)**

STEP 2        **Reflect** anything **below** the **x**-axis, in the **x**-axis, to get **y = |f(x)|**

** **

![Modulus Functions - Sketching Graphs Notes Diagram 2, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/46ef6b7b2728-2-8-4-modulus-functions-sketching-graphs-notes-d.png)

### How do I sketch functions of mod x, y = f(|x|)?

STEP 1          Sketch the graph of **y = f(x) only for *****x***** ≥ 0**

STEP 2          **Reflect** this in the ***y*****-axis**

![1-2-4-modulus-functions--sketching-graphs-notes-diagram-2-1-](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/971e683bae20-1-2-4-modulus-functions-sketching-graphs-notes-d.png)

### What is the difference between y = |f(x)| and y = f(|x|)?

- There is a difference between ***y***** = |f(*****x*****)|** and ***y***** = f(|*****x*****|)**
- The graph of** *****y***** = |f(*****x*****)| never **goes **below** the **x-axis**

  - It does not have to have any lines of symmetry
- The graph of ***y***** = f(|*****x*****|) **is **always** **symmetrical** about the ***y*****-axis**

  - It can go below the *y*-axis

![Modulus Functions - Sketching Graphs Notes Diagram 4, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/bc22611560a4-2-8-4-modulus-functions-sketching-graphs-notes-d.png)

# Solving Equations with Modulus Functions

## Modulus Functions - Solving Equations

> **Spec point** — `1.3`

## Solving equations with modulus functions

### How do I sketch modulus equations?

- Two non-parallel straight-line graphs would intersect **once**
- If a **modulus** is involved there **could** be **more** than one intersection
- **Deducing** where these **intersections** are is crucial to solving equations

- STEP 1        **Sketch** the graphs including any **modulus** (reflected) parts

  - (see Modulus Functions – Sketching Graphs)

- STEP 2        **Locate** the graph **intersections**

# Improper Algebraic Fractions

## Improper Algebraic Fractions

> **Spec point** — `1.1`

## Improper algebraic fractions

### What are improper algebraic fractions?

- The **degree** of the numerator is **greater than** or **equal** to the degree of the denominator

![Top Heavy Rational Expressions Notes Diagram 1, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/8690abd6ade2-2-6-2-top-heavy-rational-expressions-notes-diagr.png)

### How do I simplify improper algebraic fractions?

![Top Heavy Rational Expressions Notes Diagram 2, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/3dcd7e68b654-2-6-2-top-heavy-rational-expressions-notes-diagr.png)

- Write as a **quotient** and a **remainder**
- The algebraic equivalent of changing a top-heavy fraction to a mixed number

![Top Heavy Rational Expressions Notes Diagram 3, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/5b2db00887ea-2-6-2-top-heavy-rational-expressions-notes-diagr.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> Remember that simple cases are sometimes the hardest to spot!
> 
> ![Top Heavy Rational Expressions Exam Tip Diagram, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/16c93073d3e1-2-6-2-top-heavy-rational-expressions-exam-tip-di.png)

> **Worked Example**
> ![Top Heavy Rational Expressions Example Diagram, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/52e848d059a8-2-6-2-top-heavy-rational-expressions-example-dia.png)

## Quadratic Divisor

> **Spec point** — `1.1`

## Quadratic divisor

### What is a quadratic divisor?

- A polynomial f(x) of ***degree*** $n$ divided by a **quadratic divisor** takes the form

  - $\frac{f \left(x\right)}{a x^{2} + b x + c} = q \left(x\right) + \frac{r \left(x\right)}{a x^{2} + b x + c}$
- The **quotient** *q* will have degree $n-2$
- The degree of the **remainder** *r* will be less than $2$

  - It could be degree 1 (linear)
  - Or it could be degree 0 (constant)

### How do I divide a polynomial by a quadratic divisor?

- You still use **polynomial division!**
- **Step 1**
Divide the ***leading term*** of the **polynomial** by the **squared term** of the **divisor**

  - This gives the **leading term** of the **quotient**
- **Step 2**
**Multiply** this term by the **divisor**
- **Step 3**
**Subtract** this from the polynomial to get a **new polynomial** with a **lower degree**
- **Continue** these steps until you have an expression with a degree lower than 2

# Chain Rule

## Chain Rule

> **Spec point** — `4.2`

## Chain rule

### What is the chain rule?

- The chain rule is a formula that allows you to differentiate **composite functions**
- If ***y*** is a function of ***u***, and ***u*** is a function of ***x***, then the **chain rule** tells us that:

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy}{du}\times\frac{du}{dx}$

- Note that because ***u*** is a function of ***x***, ***y*** is also a function of ***x***
- In **function notation, **if $y=f(g(x))$ then the chain rule can be written as:

$\frac{dy}{dx}=f'(g(x))g'(x)$

This allows us to differentiate more complicated expressions:

![Chain Rule Illustr 1_ex, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/f02ee402c6a7-7-3-3-chain-rule-illustr-1-ex.png)

### What are the special cases of the chain rule?

- It allows us to differentiate a function raised to a power:

  - $\frac{d}{dx}((f(x)^{n})=n(f(x))^{n-1}f'(x)$

![Chain Rule Illustr 3_ex, AS & A Level Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/1fd83f3ad891-7-3-3-chain-rule-illustr-3-ex.png)

- It allows us to differentiate functions that are not given in the form ***y*****= f(*****x*****):**

  - $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\frac{dx}{dy}}$** **

![Chain Rule Illustr 4_ex, AS & A Level Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/a6871eaa9cf7-7-3-3-chain-rule-illustr-4-ex.png)

- There is a useful case which is used to integrate certain functions:

  - $\frac{d}{dx}(\mathrm{ln}(f(x))=\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$

> **Exam Hint**
> - The chain rule formulae are not in the exam formulae booklet – you have to know them.
> - When using the chain rule be sure to keep your functions straight (ie which function is ***y*** and which is ***u***, or which is ***f*** and which is ***g***).

# Differentiating Reciprocal & Inverse Trig Functions

## Differentiating Reciprocal and Inverse Trig Functions

> **Spec point** — `4.2`

## Differentiating reciprocal and inverse trig functions

### How do I differentiate reciprocal trigonometric functions?

- The formulae for the derivatives of the reciprocal trigonometric functions are:

$\frac{d}{dx}(\mathrm{sec}x)=\mathrm{sec}x\mathrm{tan}x$  
$\frac{d}{dx}(\mathrm{cosec}x)=-\mathrm{cosec}x\mathrm{cot}x$ 
$\frac{d}{dx}(\mathrm{cot}x)=-\mathrm{cosec}^{2}x$

- You can derive the derivatives for **sec**, **cosec**, and **cot** using the **chain rule** and the derivatives of the basic trigonometric functions

### How do I differentiate inverse trigonometric functions?

- The formulae for the derivatives of the inverse trigonometric functions are:

$\frac{d}{dx}(\mathrm{arcsin}x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$ 
$\frac{d}{dx}(\mathrm{arc} \mathrm{cos}x)=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$ 
$\frac{d}{dx}(\mathrm{arc} \mathrm{tan}x)=\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$

- You can derive the derivatives of **arcsin**, **arccos**, and **arctan** using the reciprocal form of the **chain rule** and the derivatives of the basic trigonometric functions ![Diff Rec Inv Trig Illustr 3, AS & A Level Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/079e9606cc20-7-3-6-diff-rec-inv-trig-illustr-3.png)

title: Product Rule
bodyMd:
# Product Rule

## Product Rule

> **Spec point** — `4.2`

## Product rule

### What is the product rule?

- The product rule is a formula that allows you to differentiate a **product of two functions**
- If $y=u\timesv$** **where ***u ***and ***v***** **are functions of** *****x*** then the product rule is:

$\frac{dy}{dx}=u\frac{dv}{dx}+v\frac{du}{dx}$

- In **function notation, **if $f(x)=g(x)\timesh(x)$ then the product rule can be written as:

$f'(x)=g(x)h'(x)+h(x)g'(x)$

- The easiest way to remember the product rule is, for** **$y=u\timesv$** **where ***u ***and ***v***** **are functions of** *****x:***

$y'=uv'+vu'$

![Product Rule Eg, AS & A Level Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/e868e427904a-7-3-4-product-rule-eg.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> - The product rule formulae are NOT in the formulae booklet – you need to know them.
> - Don't confuse the **product** of two functions with a **composite** **function:**
> 
>   - The **product** of two functions is two functions **multiplied** together
>   - A **composite** function is a **function of a function**
> 
> ![Product Rule Prod Comp Illustr, AS & A Level Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/7c5b00b1ce7e-7-3-4-product-rule-prod-comp-illustr.png)
> 
> - To differentiate composite functions you need to use the **chain rule**

> **Worked Example**

title: Quotient Rule
bodyMd:
# Quotient Rule

## Quotient Rule

> **Spec point** — `4.2`

## Quotient rule

### What is the quotient rule?

- The quotient rule is a formula that allows you to differentiate a **quotient of two functions** (ie one function divided by another)
- If $y=\frac{u}{v}$ where ***u ***and ***v***** **are functions of** *****x*** then the quotient rule is:

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{v\frac{du}{dx}-u\frac{dv}{dx}}{v^{2}}$

- In **function notation, **if $f(x)=\frac{g(x)}{h(x)}$ then the quotient rule can be written as:

$f'(x)=\frac{h(x)g'(x)-g(x)h'(x)}{(h(x))^{2}}$

![Quotient Rule Eg, AS & A Level Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/21b897475fc4-7-3-5-quotient-rule-eg.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> - The quotient rule formula is in the formulae booklet – you don't have to memorise it.
> - Be careful using the formula – because of the minus sign in the numerator the order of the functions is important.
> - Look out for functions of the form $f(x)=g(x)(h(x))^{-1}$
> 
>   - You could differentiate that using a combination of the **chain rule** and the **product rule** (and it can be good practice for you to try it!)
>   - But it can also be seen as just a quotient rule question in disguise
>   
>     - $g(x)(h(x))^{-1}=\frac{g(x)}{h(x)}$

> **Worked Example**

bodyMd:
# e & ln

## "e"

> **Spec point** — `3.1`

## "e"

### What is the number "e" in maths?

- **e** is an *irrational* number, sometimes called Euler's number

  - **e ≈ 2.718**

### How do I sketch y = e<sup>x</sup>?

![e Notes fig1, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/31a3bbcb7f0f-6-1-3-e-notes-fig1.png)

- As other exponential graphs do, **y = e**<sup>**x**</sup>

  - passes through (0, 1)
  - has the x-axis as an asymptote

### What is the special property of "e"?

![e Notes fig2, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/83e9ac29519c-6-1-3-e-notes-fig2.png)

![e Notes fig3, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/3df93ed751ea-6-1-3-e-notes-fig3.png)

- **y = e**<sup>**x**</sup> has the particular property

  - **dy/dx = e**<sup>**x**</sup>
  - ie for *every* real number **x**, the gradient of **y = e**<sup>**x**</sup> is also equal to **e**<sup>**x**</sup> (see  Derivatives of Exponential Functions)

### How do I sketch y = e<sup>-x</sup>?

![e Notes fig4, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/484361008669-6-1-3-e-notes-fig4.png)

** **

- **y = e**<sup>**-x**</sup> is a reflection in the **y**-axis of **y = e**<sup>**x**</sup>

  - They are of the form **y = f(x)** and **y = f(-x)** (see  Transformations of Functions - Reflections)

### What is exponential growth and decay?

![e Notes fig5, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/54c3253d089f-6-1-3-e-notes-fig5.png)

** **

- **y = Ae**<sup>**kx**</sup> (**k > 0**) is exponential growth
- **y = Ae**<sup>**-kx**</sup> (**k > 0**) is exponential decay
- **A** is the initial value
- **k** is a (usually positive) constant
- “-“ is used in the equation making clear whether it is growth or decay

> **Worked Example**
> ![e Example fig1, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/0ebd5dc7bf95-6-1-3-e-example-fig1.png)
> 
> ![e Example fig2, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/dcc119fa7bc0-6-1-3-e-example-fig2.png)

## "ln"

> **Spec point** — `3.2`

## "ln"

### What is ln x?

- **ln** is a function that stands for **natural logarithm**
- It is a logarithm where the **base** is the constant "**e**"

  - $\mathrm{ln}x\equiv\mathrm{log}_{e}x$
  - It is important to remember that **ln** is a function and **not a number**

### What properties of ln x do I need to know?

- Using the **definition** of a **logarithm** you can see

  - $\mathrm{ln}1=0$
  - $\mathrm{ln}e=1$
  - $\mathrm{ln}e^{x}=x$
  - $\mathrm{ln}x$ is only defined for positive *x*
- As ln is a logarithm you can use the **laws of logarithms**

  - $\mathrm{ln}a+\mathrm{ln}b=\mathrm{ln}(ab)$
  - $\mathrm{ln}a-\mathrm{ln}b=\mathrm{ln}(\frac{a}{b})$
  - $n\mathrm{ln}a=\mathrm{ln}(a^{n})$
- Any logarithm can be written in terms of the natural logarithm using the **change of base** formula

  - $log_{a} b = \frac{ln b}{ln a}$

### How do I solve equations involving e<sup>x</sup> & ln x?

- The functions $e^{x}$ and $\mathrm{ln}x$ are **inverses** of each other

  - If $e^{f(x)}=g(x)$ then $f \left(x\right) = ln  g \left(x\right)$
  - If $ln  f \left(x\right) = g \left(x\right)$ then $f \left(x\right) = e^{g \left(x\right)}$
- If your equation involves "e" then try to get all the "e" terms on one side

  - If "e" terms are multiplied, you can add the powers
  
    - $e^{x}\timese^{y}=e^{x+y}$
    - You can then apply ln to both sides of the equation
  - If "e" terms are added, try transforming the equation with a substitution
  
    - For example: If $y=e^{x}$ then $e^{4x}=y^{4}$
    - You can then solve the resulting equation (usually a quadratic)
    - Once you solve for *y* then solve for *x *using the substitution formula
- If your equation involves "ln", try to combine all "ln" terms together

  - Use the laws of logarithms to combine terms into a single term
  - If you have $ln  f \left(x\right) = ln  g \left(x\right)$ then solve $f \left(x\right) = g \left(x\right)$
  - If you have $ln  f \left(x\right) = k$ then solve $f \left(x\right) = e^{k}$

> **Worked Example**
> ![3-1-1-ln-we-solution](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/7d7a37a6c435-3-1-1-ln-we-solution.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> - Always simplify your answer if you can
> 
>   - for example, $\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{ln}25=\mathrm{ln}\sqrt{25}=\mathrm{ln}5$
>   - you wouldn't leave your final answer as $\sqrt{25}$ so don't leave your final answer as $\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{ln}25$

# Using Exponentials in Modelling

## Using Exps & Logs in Modelling

> **Spec point** — `4.4`

## Using exponentials in modelling

### What is exponential modelling?

- Exponential modelling is where real-life situations are modelled using exponential growth and decay

- Exponential growth is typically used for …

  - … population (animals and humans) increase
  - … the value of an investment under *compound interest*

![Using Exps & Logs in Modelling Notes fig2, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/55fe3ba8511a-6-3-2-using-exps-logs-in-modelling-notes-fig2.png)

- Exponential decay is typically used for …

  - … levels of radioactivity
  - … quantity of a drug in a person’s bloodstream
  - … depreciation (eg value of a standard car)

![Using Exps & Logs in Modelling Notes fig1, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/1f1bb19014c4-6-3-2-using-exps-logs-in-modelling-notes-fig1.png)

- It is important to consider if a model is only relevant for a certain period of time
- Can a population increase forever?

  - Will a very old car still be worth a small amount of money?
- For example: Consider a substance that initially contains 2000 radioactive atoms where the number of radioactive atoms, N, at time, t hours, is modelled by $N=2000e^{-kt}$

  - **y** is **N**
  - **A = 2000 **– the initial number of radioactive atoms
  - **k > 0** so the negative indicates this must be exponential **decay**
  - **t** is used (rather than **x**) as the situation is time-dependent

### How do I use exponential models?

- Recognise the form of an exponential model

  - Growth **y = Ae**<sup>**kt**</sup>
  - Decay **y = Ae**<sup>**-kt**</sup>
- **A** (constant) is the starting or initial value

  - When **t = 0**, **e**<sup>**kt**</sup>** = e**<sup>**0**</sup>** = 1** so   **y = A**

- **k** (constant) determines the **rate** of growth/decay
- Many modelling problems are about **rates** **of** **change** –

  - If **y = Ae**<sup>**kt**</sup> then     **dy/dt = Ake**<sup>**kt**</sup>
  - If **y = Ae**<sup>**-kt**</sup> then     **dy/dt = -Ake**<sup>**-kt**</sup>

![Using Exps & Logs in Modelling Notes fig4, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/66efb288771e-6-3-2-using-exps-logs-in-modelling-notes-fig4.png)

# Integrating with Trigonometric Identities

## Integrating with Trigonometric Identities

> **Spec point** — `5.2`

## Integrating with trigonometric identities

### What are trigonometric identities?

![Notes trig_id_essential, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/657b257f24f3-8-2-6-notes-trig-id-essential.png)

  - Be sure to note the difference between the **±** and **∓** symbols!

### How do I know which trigonometric identities to use?

- There is no set method
- This is a matter of experience, familiarity and recognition

  - Practice as many questions as possible
  - Be familiar with trigonometric functions that can be integrated easily
  - Be familiar with common identities – especially **squared** terms
  - **sin**<sup>**2 **</sup>**x**, **cos**<sup>**2 **</sup>**x**, **tan**<sup>**2 **</sup>**x**, **cosec**<sup>**2 **</sup>**x**, **sec**<sup>**2 **</sup>**x**, **cot**<sup>**2 **</sup>**x** all appear in identities

![Notes squared_trig_id, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/469ad14fc2d5-8-2-6-notes-squared-trig-id.png)

### How do I integrate tan<sup>2</sup>x, cot<sup>2</sup>x, sec<sup>2</sup>x and cosec<sup>2</sup>x?

- The **integral** of **sec**<sup>**2**</sup>***x*** is **tan *****x***** (+c)**

  - This is because the **derivative** of tan x is sec<sup>2</sup>x
- The **integral** of **cosec**<sup>**2**</sup>***x*** is **-cot *****x***** (+c)**

  - This is because the **derivative** of cot x is -cosec<sup>2</sup>x
- The **integral** of **tan**<sup>**2**</sup>***x*** can be found by using the identity to rewrite tan<sup>2</sup>*x *before integrating:

  - 1 + tan<sup>2</sup>*x* = sec<sup>2</sup>*x*
- The **integral** of **cot**<sup>**2**</sup>***x*** can be found by using the identity to rewrite cot<sup>2</sup>*x *before integrating:

  - 1 + cot<sup>2</sup>*x* = cosec<sup>2</sup>*x*

### How do I integrate expressions involving sin x and cos x?

- For functions of the form **sin kx**, **cos kx** … see Integrating Other Functions
- **sin kx × cos kx** can be integrated using the identity for **sin 2A**

  - **sin 2A = 2sinAcosA**

![Notes sin_cos, AS & A Level Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/bf1aab0b6aa0-8-2-6-notes-sin-cos.png)

- **sin**<sup>**n **</sup>**kx cos kx** or **sin kx cos**<sup>**n **</sup>**kx** can be integrated using **reverse chain rule** or **substitution**
- Notice no identity is used here but it looks as though there should be!

![Notes sin_cos_powers, AS & A Level Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/5877f62f66c2-8-2-6-notes-sin-cos-powers.png)

- sin<sup>2 </sup>kx and cos<sup>2 </sup>kx can be integrated by using the identity for cos 2A

  - For sin<sup>2 </sup>A, cos 2A = 1 - 2sin<sup>2 </sup>A
  - For cos<sup>2 </sup>A, cos 2A = 2cos<sup>2 </sup>A – 1

![Notes sin_cos_squared, AS & A Level Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/8ff681fc6086-8-2-6-notes-sin-cos-squared.png)

## Change of Sign

## Change of sign method

### What does a change of sign mean?

- A *sign change* between f(a) to f(b) means there must be a *root* between a and b
- When an equation cannot be solved using the usual **analytical methods**, we can use change of sign to find **approximate solutions**
- We can say a root lies within a particular *interval* or is correct to a given *accuracy*
- *Bounds* can be used to show a root is correct

## Change of Sign Failure

> **Spec point** — `6.1`

## Failure of the change of sign method

### When can the change of sign method fail?

- There are certain circumstances where a **change of sign** fails to appropriately reflect the number or existence of roots
- If the interval is **too large **there may be more than one root within it

  - An **even number of roots** mean roots are missed entirely as a sign change is not identified

# x = g(x) Iteration

## x = g(x) Iteration

> **Spec point** — `6.2`

## x = g(x) iteration

### What is iteration?

- When an equation cannot be solved using the usual **analytical methods**, we can still find **approximate solutions** to a certain degree of accuracy
- **Iteration** is one way to do this, by repeatedly using each answer as the new starting value for a function, we can achieve an ever more accurate answer

### What does x<sub>n + 1 </sub>= g(x<sub>n</sub>) mean?

- Iterations are shown using the notation x<sub>n + 1 </sub>= g(x<sub>n</sub>)
- This is a **recurrence relation** where, starting with a number (x<sub>n</sub>), we will get an answer x<sub>n + 1 </sub>which we can then reuse in the original function
- Equations need to be rearranged into an **iterative formula** – ie. the form x = g(x)

- Iterations can be shown on diagrams called **staircase** or **cobweb** diagrams

title: Compound Angle Formulae
bodyMd:
# Compound Angle Formulae

## Compound Angle Formulae

> **Spec point** — `2.3`

## Compound angle formulae

### What are the compound angle formulae?

- There are six **compound angle formulae** (also known as **addition formulae**), two each for **sin**, **cos** and **tan**:
- For **sin** the +/- sign on the left-hand side **matches** the one on the right-hand side

$\mathrm{sin}(A+B)\equiv\mathrm{sin}A\mathrm{cos}B+\mathrm{cos}A\mathrm{sin}B$ $\mathrm{sin}(A-B)\equiv\mathrm{sin}A\mathrm{cos}B-\mathrm{cos}A\mathrm{sin}B$

- For **cos** the +/- sign on the left-hand side is **opposite to** the one on the right-hand side

$\mathrm{cos}(A+B)\equiv\mathrm{cos}A\mathrm{cos}B-\mathrm{sin}A\mathrm{sin}B$ $\mathrm{cos}(A-B)\equiv\mathrm{cos}A\mathrm{cos}B+\mathrm{sin}A\mathrm{sin}B$

- For **tan** the +/- sign on the left-hand side **matches** the one in the **numerator** on the right-hand side, and is **opposite to** the one in the **denominator**

$\mathrm{tan}(A+B)\equiv\frac{\mathrm{tan}A+\mathrm{tan}B}{1-\mathrm{tan}A\mathrm{tan}B}$ $\mathrm{tan}(A-B)\equiv\frac{\mathrm{tan}A-\mathrm{tan}B}{1+\mathrm{tan}A\mathrm{tan}B}$

- You can **derive** the tan identity by:

  - Writing $\mathrm{tan}(A+B)\equiv\frac{\mathrm{sin}(A+B)}{\mathrm{cos}(A+B)}$
  - Dividing the numerator and denominator by $\mathrm{cos}A\mathrm{cos}B$

> **Exam Hint**
> - All these formulae are in the formulae booklet – you don't have to memorise them.

> **Worked Example**

## Double Angle Formulae

> **Spec point** — `2.3`

## Double angle formulae

### What are the double angle formulae?

- The **double angle formulae** are derived from the 'A+B' versions of the **compound angle formulae**:

  - $sin \left(2 A\right) \equiv 2 sin A cos A$
  - $\mathrm{cos}(2A)\equiv\mathrm{cos}^{2}A-\mathrm{sin}^{2}A$
  
    - $\mathrm{cos}(2A)\equiv2\mathrm{cos}^{2}A-1$
    - $\mathrm{cos}(2A)\equiv1-2\mathrm{sin}^{2}A$
  - $\mathrm{tan}(2A)\equiv\frac{2\mathrm{tan}A}{1-\mathrm{tan}^{2}A}$

title: Harmonic Form
bodyMd:
# Harmonic Form

## R addition formulae Rcos Rsin etc

> **Spec point** — `2.3`

## Harmonic form

### What is harmonic form?

- If ***a*** and ***b*** are positive constants, then

  - ***a *****sin *****x *****+ *****b*****cos *****x*** can be rewritten as ***R *****sin (*****x *****+ α)**
  - ***a *****sin *****x *****- *****b*****cos *****x*** can be rewritten as ***R *****sin (*****x *****- α)**
  - ***a *****cos *****x *****+ *****b*****sin *****x*** can be rewritten as ***R *****cos (*****x *****- α)**
  - ***a *****cos *****x *****- *****b*****sin *****x*** can be rewritten as ***R *****cos (*****x *****+ α)**
- The forms with ***R*** and **α **are called **harmonic forms**

  - It is the reverse of expanding the right-hand side out using compound angle formulae
  - It can be seen as factorising
- In all four cases ***R *****> 0** and **0 < α < 90°**, with:

![Rcos(x+a) Illustr 1, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/912b27e3ea50-5-6-3-rcosxa-illustr-1.png)

- To find **α**,** **first divide the **b** expression by the **a** expression

  - The ***R***'s cancel
  - Use the identity sin **α** / cos **α** = tan **α**
  - You get** b / a = tan** **α **
  - Then use** tan**<sup>**-1**</sup>** (b/a) **to find **α **

### How do I write trigonometric expressions in harmonic form?

- To rewrite the expression use the appropriate **compound angle formula** and equate coefficients ![maths-homepage-image-new](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/ce86d53fd57c-maths-homepage-image-new.png)

## Identities with reciprocal trigonometric functions

### What are the reciprocal trigonometric identities?

- There are two identities with **sec**,** cosec** and **cot **that you need to know and be able to use:

  - **tan**<sup>**2**</sup>***x *****+ 1 ≡ sec**<sup>**2**</sup>***x***
  - **1 + cot**<sup>**2**</sup>***x***** ≡ cosec**<sup>**2**</sup>***x***
- These are not really 'new' identities – they can both be derived from **sin**<sup>**2**</sup>***x *****+ cos**<sup>**2**</sup>***x***** ≡ 1**

  - To derive the identity for **sec**<sup>**2**</sup>***x***  divide  **sin**<sup>**2**</sup>***x *****+ cos**<sup>**2**</sup>***x***** ≡ 1  **by **cos**<sup>**2**</sup>***x***
  - To derive the identity for **cosec**<sup>**2**</sup>***x *** divide  **sin**<sup>**2**</sup>***x *****+ cos**<sup>**2**</sup>***x***** ≡ 1  **by **sin**<sup>**2**</sup>***x***

# Trigonometric Proof

## Trigonometric Proof

> **Spec point** — `2.3`

## Trigonometric proof

### How do I prove harder identities?

- You can use trigonometric identities you already know to prove new identities
- Make sure you know the **simple trigonometric identities** and **further trigonometric identities**
- To prove an identity start on one side and proceed step by step until you get to the other side

![Trig Proof Illustr 1, A Level & AS Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/7be967a8d572-5-8-1-trig-proof-illustr-1.png)

- Clever substitution into the **compound angle formulae **can be a useful tool for proving identities

![Trig Proof Illustr 2, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/ial-maths-20-pure-3/assets/fe3df1089d31-5-8-1-trig-proof-illustr-2.png)
